document.group: MISO Large Load Addition Resource Study (LARS)

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
Midcontinent Independent System 
) 
 
Operator, Inc. 
) 
Docket No. ER27-25-000 
 
) 
 
PROTEST AND REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF THE 
AMERICAN CLEAN POWER ASSOCIATION AND  
SOUTHERN RENEWABLE ENERGY ASSOCIATION 
 
Pursuant to Rules 211 and 212 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s 
(“Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 the American Clean Power Association 
(“ACP”) and Southern Renewable Energy Association (“SREA”) (together, “Clean Energy 
Trades”) submit this protest and request for clarification regarding the Large Load Addition 
Resource Study (“LARS”) proposal filed by the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. 
(“MISO”) on October 2, 2026 (“Filing”).2 
ACP is the leading national trade association representing companies across the clean 
power industry, including developers, owners, and operators of wind, solar, and energy storage 
facilities, many of which hold or are pursuing generator interconnection requests in MISO’s 
Definitive Planning Phase (“DPP”) queue. SREA is a non-profit regional trade association that 
works to promote the responsible development and use of utility-scale wind energy, solar energy, 
energy storage, and transmission solutions throughout the South. The Clean Energy Trades’

ER27-25-000 (Oct. 2, 2026) (“Transmittal Letter”). The Filing includes redlined Tariff sheets (Tab A) and

otherwise defined herein have the meanings given in the Transmittal Letter or the MISO Tariff. ACP and 
SREA previously submitted to the Commission timely doc-less motions to intervene on October 21,2026 and 
October 7, 2026, respectively. See Doc-Less Motion to Intervene of the American Clean Power Association, 
Docket No. ER27-25-000 (Oct. 21, 2026); Doc-Less Motion to Intervene of the Southern Renewable Energy 
Association, Docket No. ER27-25-000 (Oct. 7, 2026).

2 
members include independent power producers (“IPPs”) that develop generation to serve large 
loads and that would be directly affected by both the access rules LARS establishes and the effect 
of LARS on the transmission capacity and Network Upgrade costs available to projects in the DPP. 
MISO describes LARS as a proposal that “leverages the existing success in the MISO’s 
Expedited Project Review (‘EPR’) process on the load side and lessons learned from Expedited 
Resource Additions Study (‘ERAS’) process on the generation side.”3 The structure of LARS is 
indeed similar to that of ERAS and it raises the same open access, undue discrimination, and queue 
integrity concerns that the Clean Energy Trades raised in the ERAS proceedings, which remain 
pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.4 But LARS goes 
further than ERAS in ways the Commission has never accepted. It is permanent and uncapped. It 
is untethered to any identified resource adequacy need. It hands the application and the pairing 
decision to the load-serving entity (“LSE”) rather than to MISO. And it is not what the 
Commission’s Show Cause Order described. Most fundamentally, LARS unduly discriminates 
against IPPs by failing to provide comparable access to a Commission-jurisdictional generator 
interconnection process. LARS is also an attempt to convert what was a temporary, extraordinary 
measure into a permanent feature of MISO’s operations. Further, MISO fails to justify LARS as 
an independent entity variation from the Commission’s pro forma Large Generator 
Interconnection Procedures (“LGIP”). For the reasons set forth below, the Commission should 
reject the Filing. 
 
3  
Transmittal Letter at 2. 
4  
See Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 192 FERC ¶ 61,064 (2025) (“ERAS Acceptance Order”), order 
addressing arguments raised on reh’g, 194 FERC ¶ 61,050, at P 1 & n.4 (2026) (“ERAS Rehearing Order”) 
(noting rehearing request of the Clean Energy Associations, including ACP).

3 
I. 
BACKGROUND 
A. MISO’s Initial and Revised ERAS Proposals 
On May 16, 2025, the Commission rejected MISO’s initial ERAS proposal, finding that 
MISO had “not demonstrated that its ERAS proposal is a just and reasonable and not unduly 
discriminatory or preferential approach for addressing MISO’s stated resource adequacy and 
reliability needs.”5 The Commission identified two defects. First, the proposed Tariff placed “no 
limit on the number of projects that could be entered in the ERAS process,” which could produce 
an ERAS queue with processing times “similar to the challenges with the current DPP queue” and 
“a volume of ERAS interconnection requests untethered to reliability or resource adequacy 
needs.”6 Second, MISO had not shown “how the ERAS process is sufficiently targeted to study 
only interconnection requests needed to meet the anticipated shortfall in generating capacity 
described by MISO.”7 Commissioners Rosner and See each concurred separately.8 
MISO refiled a revised ERAS proposal that the Commission accepted on July 21, 2025. 
The accepted ERAS process is capped at 68 interconnection requests, with ten reserved for IPPs 
that have agreements with entities other than LSEs and eight reserved for requests serving retail-
choice load; it requires verification by a Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authority (“RERRA”) 
of a specific resource adequacy need; and it sunsets on the earlier of August 31, 2027 or completion 
of the sixty-eighth study.9 The Commission explained that these changes “ensure the ERAS 
process is sufficiently limited in scope to swiftly address discrete, demonstrated resource adequacy

needs in a narrowly tailored fashion, and on a temporary, time-limited basis,” and that “the limited, 
one-time design of the process weighed significantly on our decision here.”10 MISO’s own witness 
in this proceeding describes ERAS as the “temporary Expedited Resource Addition Study 
(‘ERAS’) process.”11 
B. The Show Cause Order 
On June 18, 2026, the Commission instituted a proceeding under section 206 of the Federal 
Power Act (“FPA”) in Docket No. EL26-70-000.12 As relevant here, the Commission preliminarily 
found that MISO’s Tariff “appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it lacks a generator 
interconnection study process and/or generator interconnection service to reflect an 
interconnection customer’s commitment in an interconnection agreement to limit the generating 
facility’s output to minimize the impact on the transmission system while serving an electrically 
proximate large load or large co-located load.”13 The Commission defined “electrically proximate 
large load” as a large load sufficiently close to the generator’s requested point of interconnection 
(“POI”) “such that the impact on the transmission system of the combination of the generating 
facility and the load, with the exception of the transmission facilities between the two, will be 
effectively the same as if they were located at the same substation (e.g., large load that is located 
no more than two substations away from the generating facility).”14 The Commission further stated 
that, where the generating facility serves an electrically proximate large load, “we believe that the 
generator interconnection service should be of an interim nature until the interconnection customer

Service (NRIS).”15 Separately, the Commission directed MISO to file an informational report on 
proposals under consideration to address resource adequacy for new large loads.16 
C. The LARS Proposal 
MISO proposes LARS as a new, permanent study process under which a large load of at 
least 200 megawatts (“MW”) and one or more new Generating Facilities are studied in parallel, 
with the generator receiving a Large Load Generator Interconnection Agreement (“LLGIA”) for 
NRIS in approximately 120 days.17 MISO will run three LARS study periods per year, each with 
up to ten LARS Applications studied serially on a first-come, first-served basis.18 The LARS 
Application may be initiated and submitted only by the “LARS Associated Transmission 
Customer”—the entity that procures Transmission Service for the load, which MISO 
acknowledges “is often” an LSE.19 The LARS Associated Transmission Customer also pays the 
$250,000 non-refundable application deposit.20 A LARS Generating Facility need only be located 
in the same Local Resource Zone (“LRZ”) as the load, may request NRIS up to 150% of the load’s 
peak demand, and must remain paired with the load for fifteen years, after which its 
Interconnection Service continues regardless of whether the load remains.21 LARS studies will

II. 
PROTEST 
Because MISO filed LARS under FPA section 205, MISO bears the burden of 
demonstrating that its proposal is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or 
preferential.23 MISO has not carried that burden. LARS is unduly discriminatory because it makes 
the LSE the gatekeeper of a Commission-jurisdictional generator interconnection process and 
gives LSEs contracting options that IPPs do not have. It is also unjust and unreasonable on its own 
terms.  It is a permanent, uncapped priority queue untethered to any demonstrated need, it does not 
reflect the electrically proximate configuration the Show Cause Order described, and it shifts 
transmission capacity and costs away from DPP customers.  These are the same defects the 
Commission identified when it rejected MISO’s initial ERAS proposal. Finally, MISO has not 
shown that LARS satisfies the independent entity variation standard. 
A. LARS Would Unduly Discriminate Against Independent Power Producers and 
Create Opportunities for LSE Self-Dealing. 
i. Open access requires that all interconnection customers have comparable 
access to Commission-jurisdictional interconnection service. 
The Commission’s open access framework rests on the premise that a transmission 
provider must offer service to third parties on the same or comparable basis that it provides service 
to itself. In Order No. 888, the Commission required “that all public utilities must offer . . . services 
on a non-discriminatory open access basis” and explained that “[a]n open access tariff that is not 
unduly discriminatory or anticompetitive should offer third parties access on the same or 
 
22  
Transmittal Letter at 12; Drake Testimony at 14, 28-29. 
23  
16 U.S.C. § 824d; see ERAS Rejection Order, 191 FERC ¶ 61,131 at P 197.

7 
comparable basis, and under the same or comparable terms and conditions, as the transmission 
provider’s uses of the system.”24 The Commission adopted that rule because it found that 
transmission owners with generation interests have the incentive to use their control of the grid to 
favor their own resources.25 
In Order No. 2003, the Commission extended those requirements to generator 
interconnection, recognizing that interconnection is a “critical component of open access 
transmission service and thus is subject to the requirement that utilities offer comparable service 
under the [pro forma open access transmission tariff].”26 The Commission adopted standard 
procedures to “minimize opportunities for undue discrimination and expedite the development of 
new generation, while protecting reliability and ensuring that rates are just and reasonable.”27 
Central to that framework is a single, non-discriminatory generator interconnection queue 
administered by the transmission provider, to which any interconnection customer may submit a 
request on equal terms. The Commission has consistently found the comparable ability of all

U.S. 1 (2002); see also ERAS Acceptance Order, 192 FERC ¶ 61,064 at P 193 & n.483.

transmission on a basis that is inferior to that which they provide themselves.”).

8 
generator interconnection customers to submit an interconnection request to be a critical element 
of a just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory process.28 
Priority interconnection processes are, by their nature, in tension with these principles. As 
Commissioner See explained in concurring in the rejection of MISO’s initial ERAS proposal, 
“where a proposal’s goal is to get some interconnection requests through the study process faster 
than others, the Commission is by definition asked to greenlight discrimination,” and “[t]o justify 
that step under our statutory mandate, priority processes should be tailored enough to accomplish 
the identified ends.”29 The Commission likewise held that MISO “must ensure that this proposal 
is aligned with the Commission’s open access principles in an objective and transparent manner 
in order to meet the FPA’s requirements that rates be just and reasonable and not unduly 
discriminatory or preferential.”30 LARS does not meet that standard. 
ii. LARS makes the LSE the gatekeeper of a Commission-jurisdictional generator 
interconnection process. 
Unlike any generator interconnection process the Commission has accepted, an 
interconnection customer seeking LARS treatment cannot submit its request to MISO. Under 
proposed Section 3.12.1, “[t]he LARS Associated Transmission Customer initiates the submission 
of the LARS Application for the proposed load and associated generation,” and MISO confirms 
that the LARS Associated Transmission Customer “is the only party that may submit the LARS

request); Cal. Indep. Sys. Operator Corp., 188 FERC ¶ 61,225, at P 94 (2024) (“CAISO IPE Order”) 
(comparable ability to join the cluster)); Protest of the Clean Energy Associations, Docket No. ER25-1674-

Application.”31 In practice, the LARS Associated Transmission Customer will be the LSE that 
procures transmission service on behalf of the large load (hereinafter, the “LSE”). The LSE pays 
the non-refundable application deposit, designates which load is “formally paired” with which 
Interconnection Request, and decides whether any application is submitted at all.32 MISO states 
that allowing the generator and load to contract directly “does not supersede the role of the LARS 
Associated Transmission Customer to determine whether to submit a LARS Application.”33 The 
POI, in turn, must be negotiated by the Interconnection Customer with and attested to by the 
Transmission Owner before the application may be filed.34 Because MISO is primarily a vertically 
integrated region, in which the LSE and the Transmission Owner are frequently the same utility 
or affiliates, the LSE thus controls the generator-side application process entirely. 
Even an IPP with a direct offtake agreement with the large load must be sponsored by the 
LSE’s application; there is no path for an IPP to deal directly with MISO for purposes of accessing 
the generator interconnection queue. And in most MISO states, retail service laws prohibit an IPP 
from contracting to serve the load directly—a point MISO itself acknowledges by adding Tariff 
language providing that LARS does not authorize a generator that is not an LSE to serve load 
where state law does not allow it.35 In those states, the IPP’s only possible counterparty is the same 
utility that controls the application and that may compete to self-build the generation. To be clear, 
the Clean Energy Trades’ concern is with ensuring that access to a Commission-jurisdictional 
generator interconnection process is not unduly discriminatory, consistent with the Commission’s

open access principles. The Clean Energy Trades fully acknowledge that certain state laws in 
MISO restrict third-party competitive generation from serving retail load and the Clean Energy 
Trades do not seek to change those laws or to expand retail competition through this proceeding. 
The Commission has recognized that utilities with generation interests have the incentive 
to discriminate when given the opportunity. Indeed, that is the premise of Order Nos. 888 and 
2003, and of the independent entity variation itself.36 The concern is particularly acute in MISO, 
which, as Commissioner See observed, “is largely comprised of vertically integrated States.” 
Illinois and part of Michigan are the only retail choice jurisdictions in MISO.37 The Commission 
addressed this very risk in ERAS, where MISO reserved ten slots for IPPs with agreements with 
entities other than LSEs specifically “to address claims that LSEs could block independent power 
producers from participating in the ERAS process,” and eight slots for retail-choice load.38 The 
Commission relied on those carve-outs to find that “all interconnection customers will have 
comparable ability to seek to participate in the ERAS process, regardless of location and ownership 
type.”39 ERAS also required a RERRA to verify the need for each project, including LSE self-
supply projects.40 LARS has no carve-out, no RERRA or other regulatory check, and no scoring 
criteria. 
While it is reasonable for LSEs to initiate and oversee LARS requests on the load side, 
given state jurisdiction over retail service and LSEs’ obligations to serve load, that logic does not

extend to the generation side, where generator interconnection procedures fall within the 
Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction and are subject to open access requirements.41 Nothing 
prevents MISO from allowing an interconnection customer to initiate the generator portion of a 
LARS Application directly with MISO, with an obligation on the LSE and Transmission Owner 
to respond. Stakeholders asked MISO to do exactly that and MISO declined without explanation.42 
Allowing incumbent LSEs to gain complete control of the entry point to a new, expedited generator 
interconnection process is inconsistent with the Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction over 
generator interconnection and with its open access rules. 
iii. LARS does not offer interconnection service on a comparable and non-
discriminatory basis to similarly situated interconnection customers. 
The designation of the LSE as the sole entity that may submit an application is not the only 
obstacle to open access. LARS’ eligibility requirements also discriminate against third-party 
competitive generation. Every LARS application requires an executed, binding agreement between 
the Interconnection Customer and either the LSE or the entity that owns or controls the load.43 
Even in the hypothetical scenario in which an LSE agrees to incorporate a third party’s 
Interconnection Request into its LARS application, the third party must produce either a power 
purchase agreement (“PPA”) or similar offtake agreement with the load, or a Build-Own-Transfer

agreement transferring the facility to the LSE or load.44 An LSE, however, may instead rely on 
“evidence of other types of agreements that provide that the generation is intended to serve the 
LARS Associated Load customer,” including “a special contract, a large load tariff agreement, or 
retail service agreement.”45 MISO’s witness explains that this third option was added specifically 
to accommodate “specific utility arrangements with large loads where the LSE business model 
uses one or more agreements that are not traditional PPAs.”46 LSEs are thus afforded far more 
flexible means of qualifying than are IPPs. 
Comparable flexibility for third parties is necessary both to avoid undue discrimination and 
to provide commercially viable options. Requiring an executed PPA as a condition of entry into 
an interconnection process is inconsistent with the project development life cycle. In Order No. 
2023, the Commission declined to adopt the non-financial commercial readiness demonstrations 
proposed in the NOPR—which included executed contracts—recognizing that such 
demonstrations “may be unavailable to interconnection customers with commercially viable 
projects,” for example “as a result of a misalignment of the timing between resource procurement 
decisions and interconnection study processes.”47 Network Upgrade costs were not known at the 
time of an ERAS application and they will not be known at the time of a LARS application; an 
IPP must commit to binding offtake terms without knowing its interconnection costs, while the 
LSE may rely on a retail tariff arrangement whose costs can be passed through to ratepayers.

The Clean Energy Trades recognize that, in ERAS, the Commission found that a similar 
distinction between IPP agreement options and LSE self-supply did not render the proposal unjust 
and unreasonable.48 But the Commission reached that conclusion because LSE self-supply under 
ERAS “must still be verified by a RERRA,” because ERAS reserved slots for IPPs with non-LSE 
agreements, and because the process was limited in duration and size.49 None of those safeguards 
exists in LARS. The ERAS agreement requirement was also more flexible for IPPs than the LARS 
requirement. Under ERAS, any interconnection customer—including an IPP—could satisfy the 
requirement through an “other” executed agreement, an option MISO added to establish “a 
minimum requirement that an arrangement exists between the driver of the need and the project to 
address that need,” and which the Commission found “provides considerable flexibility for 
interconnection customers, including independent power producers.”50 LARS includes a similar 
catch-all—“other types of agreements that provide that the generation is intended to serve the 
LARS Associated Load customer”—but makes it available only to LSEs and Alternative Retail 
Electric Suppliers.51 That IPPs were able to participate in ERAS therefore says little about whether 
they can do so on comparable terms under LARS. 
The practical result of these restrictions on open access will be (1) a reduction in the pool 
of supply options with timely GIAs available to large load offtakers and for state consideration in 
competitive solicitation processes; (2) the ability of LSE self-supply to drive the cost of new 
generation serving large loads; and (3) the general elimination of visibility into the pricing of

alternative generation that could have obtained timely GIAs on comparable terms. MISO’s 
assurance that LARS is “open to all Interconnection Customers that meet the Tariff’s 
requirements” does not answer these concerns, because the Tariff’s requirements themselves are 
what deny comparable access.52 
B. LARS Is Not Just and Reasonable. 
i. LARS is a permanent, uncapped expedited queue untethered to any identified 
need, unlike every expedited interconnection process the Commission has 
accepted. 
The Show Cause Order did not direct MISO to create a separate, permanent, expedited 
generator interconnection queue. The Commission expressed concern about the absence of “a 
generator interconnection study process and/or generator interconnection service” reflecting a 
generator’s commitment to limit its output while serving an electrically proximate large load.53 
The Commission did not require that such a process operate outside of, or ahead of, the DPP, and 
it stated that service to a generator serving an electrically proximate large load “should be of an 
interim nature until the interconnection customer obtains [ERIS] or [NRIS].”54 LARS does the 
opposite: it grants permanent NRIS through a parallel process that MISO describes as “a 
permanent MISO study process.”55 Moreover, the Filing makes clear that even where the paired 
LARS Associated Load ceases taking service, or the agreement pairing the generator and the load 
terminates, during the fifteen-year pairing period, the LARS generator may continue to operate 
under its LLGIA—subject to MISO’s Annual ERIS and Quarterly Operating Limit processes—

not only for a one-year transition period, but for as long as DPP processing of its new 
Interconnection Request is delayed beyond that year.56 In effect, this work-around creates an 
exclusive pathway for LSE-selected generators to leverage their access to LARS to obtain 
expedited interconnection that persists even after the paired load is gone, undermining the very 
basis for granting those generators priority access in the first place. 
Nor did the Show Cause Order’s invitation for resource adequacy proposals relax the FPA 
section 205 standard. The Commission directed MISO to report on proposals under consideration 
to address resource adequacy for new large loads and “strongly encourage[d] new proposals to the 
extent necessary to address these concerns.”57 An invitation to propose solutions is not a pre-
approval of whatever MISO proposes and it does not displace the Commission’s consistent 
requirement that priority interconnection processes be bounded and tailored to an identified need. 
Every expedited interconnection process the Commission has accepted has been bounded. 
In PJM’s Reliability Resource Initiative (“RRI”), PJM specified that it would study no more than 
50 projects on a one-time basis, “providing clear bounds in its tariff.”58 The revised MISO ERAS 
process is capped at 68 requests and sunsets no later than August 31, 2027—limits that remained 
in place even when the Commission later accepted an increase in the number of requests MISO 
may study each quarter.59 SPP’s ERAS was a one-time process that limited the capacity that may 
participate through a formula tied to each participating load-responsible entity’s resource adequacy

deficiency.60 SPP’s High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (“HILLGA”)—the model 
the Show Cause Order itself discussed—is an “interim” service that the Commission accepted as 
“a flexible, expedited, and separate serial interconnection process that will facilitate the prompt 
interconnection of generating facilities that are limited to serving a [High Impact Large Load

relationship with an LSE, not by any reduced impact on the grid.

D. MISO Has Not Demonstrated That LARS Satisfies the Independent Entity 
Variation Standard. 
In Order No. 2003, the Commission permitted RTOs and ISOs to propose “independent 
entity variations” from the pro forma LGIP and LGIA, recognizing that an RTO or ISO “has 
different operating characteristics depending on its size and location and is less likely to act in an 
unduly discriminatory manner than a Transmission Provider that is a market participant.”112 Under 
that standard, an RTO/ISO must demonstrate that its proposed variations “are just and reasonable 
and not unduly discriminatory or preferential and accomplish the purposes of Order No. 2003.”113 
The flexibility the standard affords rests on the RTO/ISO’s independence. Although RTOs have 
far less incentive to discriminate, the same cannot be said of the LSEs and Transmission Owners 
to which LARS delegates control. 
LARS deviates from at least three core elements of the pro forma LGIP. First, under the 
pro forma LGIP, an interconnection customer submits its interconnection request directly to the 
transmission provider, and the transmission provider—not a third party—administers access to 
interconnection service.114 LARS instead requires that the request be submitted by the LSE, and it 
requires a POI agreed to and attested by the Transmission Owner before the request may be 
filed.115 Second, the pro forma LGIP establishes a single queue in which requests are studied on

MISO does not attempt to justify these deviations under the independent entity variation

Because MISO itself is not the entity to which the generator submits its LARS application, and

Because the LSE is the gatekeeper of LARS in a way that goes beyond even the initial ERAS 
proposal, MISO cannot satisfy the independent entity variation standard, and LARS does not 
accomplish the purposes of Order No. 2003: to “minimize opportunities for undue discrimination 
and expedite the development of new generation.”120

III. 
REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION 
If the Commission does not reject the Filing, it should direct MISO to clarify whether the 
LARS same-LRZ requirement applicable to a LARS Interconnection Customer is determined 
based on a Generating Facility’s physical location or on its POI to the MISO Transmission System. 
Proposed Attachment X, Section 3.12.2 appears to apply the same-LRZ requirement based on the 
Generating Facility’s POI for an individual LARS Interconnection Customer, providing that “[t]he 
Point of Interconnection specified in a LARS Application must be located in the same Local 
Resource Zone as the Point of Withdrawal of the LARS Associated Load.”121 However, where 
multiple Generating Facilities serve a single LARS Associated Load behind different POIs, the 
proposed Tariff states that the Generating Facilities must “[b]e located in the same LRZ as the 
LARS Associated Load,” creating ambiguity as to whether the requirement applies to the physical 
location of the Generating Facilities or to their respective POIs.122 
The Clean Energy Trades request that the Commission direct MISO to clarify that, for 
purposes of the same-LRZ requirement, the relevant location is the applicable POI to the MISO 
Transmission System rather than the physical location of the Generating Facility, including where 
multiple Generating Facilities serve a single LARS Associated Load. 
IV. 
CONCLUSION 
For the reasons stated above, the Clean Energy Trades respectfully request that the 
Commission reject MISO’s LARS proposal. In the event the Commission accepts any portion of 
the Filing, the Clean Energy Trades request that the Commission direct MISO to provide the 
clarification requested in Part III above.
